title: Stentrode endovascular brain-computer interface lets two people with ALS text, shop and manage finances independently at home
summary: Two ALS participants in Melbourne used a Stentrode BCI with ML click decoding for unsupervised home texting, shopping and banking.
account: Two people with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and flaccid upper-limb paralysis received the Stentrode at the Royal Melbourne Hospital. The Stentrode is an electrode array delivered via the jugular vein into the superior sagittal sinus. The first-in-human study is in the Journal of NeuroInterventional Surgery (published online 28 October 2020). Participant 1 was implanted in mid-2019 and participant 2 in early 2020. The paper gives no exact event dates. Machine-learning-assisted training mapped attempted-movement electrocorticography to mouse clicks, combined with an eye-tracker for cursor navigation. Unsupervised home use then began on day 86 for participant 1 and day 71 for participant 2. Click accuracies were 92.63% and 93.18%, and they typed 13.81 and 20.10 correct characters per minute. They independently did text messaging, online shopping and managing finances. The hospital's statement of 29 October 2020 confirms these activities.
purpose: Restore digital device control for people with severe paralysis without open-brain surgery
system: Synchron Stentrode endovascular brain-computer interface with machine-learning click decoder and eye-tracker cursor navigation
model_version: Stentrode first-in-human system (early feasibility trial, Clinicaltrials.gov NCT03834857)
developer: Synchron Inc. with the University of Melbourne
deployer: Royal Melbourne Hospital (implantation and follow-up); participants' homes (use)
segment: People with ALS and severe upper-limb paralysis

ratings.reason: Two identified participants regained independent texting, shopping and money management at home. An eye-tracker handled cursor navigation, so the BCI's own contribution is the click control.
First-in-human feasibility in two people. Later SWITCH follow-up covered four patients with no serious adverse events, still a small cohort.

ai_role.statement: Per the paper, a machine-learning-assisted decoder (binary SVM or threshold classifier on spectral power) detected attempted movements and generated click commands. Cursor navigation came from an eye-tracker, so the AI contribution is the click selection channel, which the authors report with 92–93% accuracy.

headline: Stentrode BCI lets two men with ALS text and shop at home
metric: typed 13.81 and 20.10 correct characters per minute

comparator.against: a previous fully implanted BCI requiring burr hole craniotomy
comparator.before: 197 days of training prior to unsupervised home use and achieved a single binary click
comparator.after: unsupervised home use of multiple-click actions within 86 days (participant 1) and 71 days (participant 2) of neurointerventional surgery
comparator.quote: The current study achieved unsupervised home use of multiple-click actions within 86 days (participant 1) and 71 days (participant 2) of neurointerventional surgery.

later.note: The SWITCH study reported four implanted patients completing 12-month follow-up without serious adverse events, and the trial continued in the United States with more participants planned.
later.quote: Each completed 12-month follow-up with no serious adverse events and no vessel occlusion or device migration.
